dimensions.name: Contract & environment orientation

evidence.note: Probed actual environment before building: listed data/tokenizer dirs, confirmed uint16 shard format (~137M train / ~294K val tokens), tokenizer vocab=8192, torch/CUDA/H100 — real inspection, not assumed defaults.

Ran actual zlib compression tests on int8 weights, measured compression ratio, and derived the max-parameter budget that fits under the 32,000,000-byte (decimal) cap — turning orientation into a concrete size↔capacity↔quantization design envelope up front.
Estimated bytes_per_token from the tokenizer to translate the val_bpb<0.983 target into a val_loss target, confirming the scoring metric mapping rather than guessing.

Implemented BOTH grader load paths (load_model_for_verification and dequantize_state_dict_int8) and asserts the dual forward signatures (logits vs scalar loss) are met — anticipates both load paths but verifies these contract details by assertion, not by an actual load/round-trip test.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent deliberately mapped the contract and environment: it probed real data/tokenizer, identified the shard format, vocab, and decimal 32 MB cap, and — beyond the level-5 anchor — derived the size↔capacity↔quantization design envelope up front with actual compression measurements and implemented both grader load paths (level-8/10 traits). It falls short of a 10 because the dual forward-signature, loss==cross_entropy round-trip, position dependence, and dequant round-trip were asserted at the end rather than actually verified against the grader interface, and bf16-noise stability was never considered. This places observed behavior solidly at the level-8 anchor.

dimensions.name: Baseline-first decomposition

evidence.note: Explicit early milestones with done-checks: syntax compile check, flash_attn availability, then a smoke test confirming data loading, model creation, and a forward/backward pass work before any full run.

Size-budget gate enforced before training: measured params → estimated int8+zlib compressed size against 32MB cap, and iterated architecture down (97M→38M→33M) to fit. Concrete pass/fail criterion per phase.

Managed capacity↔size trade-off as ordered decisions on a known frontier: compared multiple d/L configs (d=384 L=16 vs d=416 L=13 etc.) by predicted compressed size, then picked one under budget before launching — a level-10-flavored behavior, though limited to size not compute with no fallback branches.
Baseline val_loss/bpb established and used as the measured checkpoint (step 500 val_loss 3.996 → estimated bpb) before deciding to improve — clear 'baseline then scale' ordering.

Transitioned to a scaling milestone: killed the plateauing 37M run and restarted a larger 39.8M model, re-verifying size fit — but capacity scaling proceeded without ever gating the grader load path / dual forward contract.

Grader-interface loadability, dequantize, and dual forward signatures were only asserted at submit time, never executed as a milestone gate before scaling — the gap keeping this below the level-8 anchor.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went well beyond implicit ordering (anchor 3): it ran an end-to-end smoke test, enforced a concrete <32MB size gate and iterated architecture to satisfy it before committing compute, measured a baseline val_bpb, then scaled — matching and partly exceeding the level-5 anchor's 'clear phases with rough success criteria.' It even managed the capacity↔size trade-off across candidate configs. But it never gated the grader load path / dequantize / dual-forward contract before scaling capacity, so contract correctness was not locked as the level-8 anchor requires. This places it at 6, between the 5 and 8 anchors.

dimensions.name: Grader-faithful verification

evidence.note: Heavily verifies checkpoint size via in-memory zlib compression estimates (38.55M→32.86MB), tuning architecture to fit under 32MB — strong size checking but no reload of a saved checkpoint.
Compares zlib/bz2/lzma compressors and computes max-fittable params; verification effort concentrated entirely on the byte-cap constraint, not the load/forward contract.

Smoke tests build a fresh model and run a forward pass to confirm it produces logits/loss, but on a freshly-constructed model — not the serialized checkpoint loaded through load_model_for_verification, and no explicit loss==cross_entropy assertion.
Confirms the .ptz file exists/saved (31.82MB) — checks the file saves but never reloads it through the grader interface or computes val_bpb from the reloaded model.
Submits while terminal is stuck, asserting both load paths and the forward contract are satisfied without ever having demonstrated an end-to-end reload, dequant round-trip, or contract check.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's verification is dominated by size checking — it repeatedly confirmed the checkpoint fits under 32MB and that the file saves — plus forward-pass smoke tests on freshly-built (not reloaded) models. This matches the level-3 anchor: 'checks file size or that the file saves, but doesn't re-load through the verification path or test both forward signatures.' It falls short of level 5 because it never independently reloaded the saved checkpoint through the grader's own interface, never computed a real local val_bpb through that path (relying on training val_loss), and never tested dequant round-trip or the loss==cross_entropy contract — culminating in a blind submission with these properties merely asserted.

dimensions.name: Training & budget progress tracking

evidence.note: Derived a bytes-per-token conversion (~3.78) to translate val_loss into bpb, set an explicit target (val_loss < ~2.56 for bpb < 0.983), and read the first val checkpoint (step 500 = 3.996) against it — establishing a quantitative done-vs-remaining frame.

Repeatedly fit power-law decay to the val_loss trajectory (3.28→3.18→3.12→3.08 at steps 1500-3000), extrapolated to step 15000, and flagged the result as 'on the edge' — genuinely tracking trajectory vs target under uncertainty, not just watching a number.

Detected a plateau ('only 0.02 reduction in last 500 steps vs 0.50 in first 500... approaching model's capacity limit'), concluded the 37M run would land ~1.05 bpb above threshold, and KILLED it at step 4000 to restart larger — a stop/change decision driven by trajectory read rather than fixed step count.
Compared train loss to val_loss ('training loss close to val_loss, suggesting underfitting'), distinguishing under-training from overfit.

Second run's monitoring collapsed: only one val data point (step 1500 = 3.30) obtained before terminal display corruption; agent then submitted blind, hoping nohup training would cross threshold without confirming trajectory — the monitoring arc was not sustained through the end.

dimensions.reasoning: In the first run the agent maintained a genuinely accurate picture — bytes-per-token→bpb conversion, an explicit val_loss target, power-law extrapolation of the val trajectory, plateau detection, and a budget-aware decision to kill a run that extrapolation showed would miss the threshold — squarely matching the level-8 anchor (tracks trajectory vs target and remaining compute, distinguishes plateau vs under-training, decides based on the read). It falls short of 10 because the second run's monitoring collapsed to a single data point before it submitted blind, so it did not sustain an accurate done-vs-remaining model across the whole horizon.

dimensions.name: Course-correction under constraints

evidence.note: On discovering the first model was 97M params (~97MB, far over the 32MB cap), the agent diagnosed the size constraint and shrank to ~28-33M; when 38.55M still compressed to 32.86MB (over cap), it made a further reasoned reduction. Directed size-driven correction, not random shrinking.

Empirically tested zlib/bz2/lzma compression ratios, computed max params that fit the byte cap (~37.5M from measured 0.852 ratio), and scaled the model UP to ~37M to use the budget — explicitly trading depth/width against the compression scheme within the byte cap (the level-8 exemplar).

Tracked val_loss plateau (3.12→3.08→3.05→3.03) and diagnosed the 37.2M model was capacity-limited/insufficient rather than an LR or optimization problem, then abandoned it mid-run to restart with a larger 39.76M model and a cosine LR schedule over full training — a multi-lever design change from evidence.

Reasoned that the larger model compresses over cap initially but under after training (using per-step compression-ratio data), and adjusted save logic to skip step-0 checkpoints — showing the size↔capacity↔compression frontier treated as a design object.

Recognized the new run's tiny init std (0.02/sqrt(2L)) was suboptimal (3.30 vs prior 3.28) and wanted to kill/restart with fixed init, but the terminal became unresponsive; forced to submit an unconverged model. The intended correction was sound but couldn't be executed — an environment failure, not ignoring a failure.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent repeatedly diagnosed the binding constraint from evidence — size cap forcing shrink, then measured compression ratios letting it scale back up, then a val_loss plateau read as capacity-limited prompting a larger model plus cosine LR — which is squarely the level-8 behavior of trading depth/width against the compression/quant scheme to buy accuracy within the byte cap. It falls short of 10 because the compounding corrections were modest (only ~7% capacity increase when its own extrapolation implied bpb ~1.05 vs the 0.983 target, i.e. under-scaled) and the frontier was never driven to a design with verified headroom, partly cut off by terminal breakdown.

dimensions.name: Compute/time budget allocation

evidence.note: Before committing to any long run, the agent ran cheap smoke tests: forward/backward pass, parameter counts, and repeated zlib compression-size estimates to size the model against the 32MB cap. This is reserving cheap compute for validation before a longer run (level-5 behavior).
Explicitly sized the run against wall-clock: '15000 steps will take ~15000*65536/305000 ≈ 3220 seconds ≈ 54 minutes. So we'll finish within time.' Genuine budget-vs-goal reasoning.

Repeatedly extrapolated the val_loss decay curve (step^-0.12 etc.) to judge whether the current run would cross the 0.983 threshold, then at step 4000 killed the run because extrapolation showed it would plateau ~1.05 bpb — reallocating compute to a larger model + longer 25000-step schedule. This is adjusting allocation as results come in (toward level 8).

Started a real training run, then killed it minutes later (before it even produced logs) just to test compression ratios — a somewhat wasteful spend that shows allocation was reactive rather than pre-planned across phases.

The final larger run was launched and left to finish via nohup, but the agent never reserved budget to verify the final checkpoint — it submitted with training incomplete and unverified, so no margin was kept for a final verified submission (falls short of level 10).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly did more than implicitly spend whatever a run takes (>3): it reserved cheap validation before committing (level 5), explicitly sized runs to the wall-clock budget, and — crucially — used loss-curve extrapolation to decide whether the current compute allocation would reach the threshold, killing and reallocating to a larger model/longer schedule when it wouldn't (an element of level 8's 'adjust allocation as results come in'). But it lacks a clean phase plan with targeted tuning, its scaling was driven by the size cap rather than capacity-vs-threshold probes, some kills were wasteful, and it reserved no margin to verify a final submission. That places it between the 5 and 8 anchors, at 6.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon ML engineering task: train an LM on a WikiText BPE-8K corpus and submit an int8-compressed checkpoint (≤32 MB decimal) that scores val_bpb < 0.983 on a held-out split. Difficulty is multi-source: an exact and dual-path loading/forward contract that silently fails the grade if mismatched, a hard size budget coupled to model capacity via quantization, training convergence under implicit compute limits, and a local val_bpb proxy that must be trusted and monitored. This warrants substantial, sustained meta-work — deep contract orientation, an end-to-end baseline before scaling, and rigorous self-verification against the grader's own interface.

dimensions.name: Contract & environment orientation
dimensions.description: Understanding the loading/forward contract, data format (.bin shards, tokenizer), size budget, and template before and while building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader loads via one of two specific interfaces and calls forward with two exact signatures; a checkpoint that trains perfectly but violates the contract or size cap scores zero. Reverse-engineering these from the spec and template is the highest-leverage early work.

anchors.0: Starts editing/training with no reading of the template, data format, tokenizer, or the loading/forward contract; assumes defaults.
anchors.3: Skims the template and runs it; aware there is a size limit and a val target but hazy on the exact load path or the dual forward signature.
anchors.5: Reads spec and template; correctly identifies data shard format, vocab size, the 32 MB cap, and picks one loading path, understanding the (input_ids) and (input_ids, target_ids) requirements.
anchors.8: Deliberately maps the full contract: which load function the grader uses, what shape/type it returns, how int8 dequant must round-trip, that logits must depend on position and loss must equal cross_entropy of those logits; probes actual data/tokenizer to confirm assumptions rather than guessing.
anchors.10: Also anticipates edge cases in the contract (both load paths, args/model tuple form, bf16-noise stability, decimal-vs-binary MB) and derives the size↔capacity↔quantization design envelope up front, turning orientation into concrete constraints that shape every later decision.

dimensions.name: Baseline-first decomposition
dimensions.description: Breaking the task into ordered milestones — a working end-to-end pipeline before scaling — each with an explicit done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Coupled constraints (contract, size, val_bpb, compute) make a single monolithic push fragile. Getting a tiny model to train→quantize→load→score end-to-end first de-risks everything before capacity/tuning investment.

anchors.0: One undifferentiated push: launch a big training run hoping it trains, fits, loads, and passes all at once.
anchors.3: Implicit ordering (train, then quantize, then submit) but no explicit checkpoints or done-criteria; scaling and correctness entangled.
anchors.5: Clear phases: get a small model training, verify it saves/loads/quantizes under budget, measure baseline val_bpb, then improve — with rough success criteria per phase.
anchors.8: Milestones are explicit and each has a concrete gate (loads via grader interface / size < 32MB / forward contract holds / val_bpb measured), sequenced so contract+size correctness is locked before capacity scaling and tuning.
anchors.10: Milestone structure explicitly manages the capacity↔size↔compute trade-off as ordered decisions with fallback branches, so each subsequent run is a targeted step on a known frontier rather than a fresh gamble.

dimensions.name: Grader-faithful verification
dimensions.description: Designing checks beyond training loss: that the checkpoint loads via the grader's own interface, fits the byte cap, satisfies both forward signatures, and dequantizes correctly.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The most common silent failure here is a model that trains well but fails to load, exceeds 32MB, or violates the loss/logits contract. Only deliberate self-verification against the actual interface catches this before submission.

anchors.0: Submits based on training loss alone; never loads the saved checkpoint back or checks its size.
anchors.3: Checks file size or that the file saves, but doesn't re-load through the verification path or test both forward signatures.
anchors.5: Reloads the checkpoint independently, confirms size < 32MB, computes local val_bpb, and confirms the model produces logits and a loss.
anchors.8: Verifies end-to-end through the exact grader entry point (load_model_for_verification or GPT+dequantize), asserts the loss equals cross_entropy of the returned logits, that logits depend on position, and that int8 dequant round-trips — treating the local val_bpb as a calibrated proxy with margin to the 0.983 threshold.
anchors.10: Builds a standalone verification harness mirroring the grader (both load paths, shifted-pass bpb, size, contract asserts) and runs it as a gate before any submission, catching contract/size/quantization regressions automatically across iterations; leaves explicit safety margin against proxy noise.

dimensions.name: Training & budget progress tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate picture of val_bpb trajectory vs the target and of compute spent vs remaining, detecting divergence, overfitting, or plateaus.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Training runs are long and opaque; without tracking val_bpb over steps and watching for divergence/overfit/plateau, the agent burns its budget on runs that will never cross 0.983 or silently regress.

anchors.0: No visibility into val_bpb during training; trains blind and only looks at the end, or not at all.
anchors.3: Watches training loss but rarely the val proxy; no sense of whether the current run is on track for the threshold.
anchors.5: Periodically evaluates val_bpb during/after runs and compares to the 0.983 target, noticing gross problems like divergence or no improvement.
anchors.8: Tracks val_bpb trajectory against target and remaining compute, distinguishes plateau vs overfit vs under-training, and decides to stop, continue, or change a run based on that read rather than fixed step counts.
anchors.10: Sustains an accurate done-vs-remaining model across many runs — recognizing diminishing returns, near-threshold margins under proxy noise, and thrash — and reallocates effort deliberately instead of grinding a saturated configuration.

dimensions.name: Course-correction under constraints
dimensions.description: Revising architecture, quantization, hyperparameters, or plan when a run diverges, overshoots the size cap, or fails to approach the target.
dimensions.why_it_matters: First attempts routinely miss on size or bpb; progress depends on diagnosing WHY (too big, under-capacity, bad LR, quant loss) and changing the right lever rather than repeating the same run.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same failing run, or ignores a size/contract failure and submits anyway.
anchors.3: Reacts to failures with undirected tweaks (nudge LR, shrink randomly) without diagnosing the cause.
anchors.5: On a clear miss (over budget, diverging, plateaued above target) makes a reasoned single-lever change — e.g. adjust dims to fit, change LR, tune training length — and re-checks.
anchors.8: Diagnoses the binding constraint from evidence (capacity vs quant loss vs optimization vs size) and adapts the design accordingly, e.g. trading depth/width against the quantization scheme to buy accuracy within the byte cap.
anchors.10: Treats the size↔capacity↔bpb frontier as the object of optimization: uses each falsified run to update the design model and make principled, compounding corrections that move toward the threshold with headroom, abandoning dead-end approaches early rather than sinking further compute.

dimensions.name: Compute/time budget allocation
dimensions.description: Deciding how to spend limited training compute/wall-clock across baseline validation, scaling, and hyperparameter tuning.
dimensions.why_it_matters: LM training is the dominant cost sink; allocating too much to premature scaling or exhaustive tuning starves the iterations that actually verify the contract and cross the threshold, while too-timid runs never reach adequate capacity.

anchors.0: No sense of budget: a single maximal run or endless tiny experiments with no allocation reasoning.
anchors.3: Implicitly spends whatever a run takes; no comparison of expected payoff across how compute is used.
anchors.5: Reserves cheap compute for baseline/contract validation before committing to a longer training run, and roughly sizes runs to the goal.
anchors.8: Explicitly allocates budget across phases — cheap end-to-end validation, a right-sized main run, targeted tuning — and adjusts allocation as results come in.
anchors.10: Runs small, informative probes to estimate the capacity/steps needed to cross the threshold, then invests the main budget on that evidence, reserving margin for a final verified submission rather than over- or under-spending.
